unmapped_findings: For the 2.5 Al alloy, applying the Williams and Carter correction for partial dislocation strain fields would increase the SFE to 44.0 ± 9.8 mJ m⁻² (uncorrected value 38.3 ± 6.1 mJ m⁻²); the correction was not applied. [b0029]

The Al-induced SFE increase for the 2.5 Al alloy relative to the base alloy is reported as 12.0 mJ m⁻² in the results/discussion (b0029), while the abstract/conclusion give a range of 12–17 mJ m⁻² (b0006, b0034).
Accounting for the partial dislocation strain-field correction yields an estimated A_Al^SFE value of 6.9 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ in this study, compared with the uncorrected 4.9 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹. [b0033]
The 2.5 Al alloy composition (wt.%) from Table 1: C 0.030, N 0.0034, Ni 15.04, Cr 11.02, Mn 1.08, Si 0.034, Al 2.47; solution annealed at 1060 °C. [b0015]

Ignoring the effect of Al on the austenite lattice parameter can overestimate the calculated austenite C content by δ_C ≈ 0.125–0.176 wt.% (assuming x_Al = 1 wt.%), i.e. on the order of 0.15 wt.% in Al-alloyed AHSS. [b0026, b0034]

Using effective elastic constants for a 12 Ni–12 Cr steel (G = 66 GPa, ν = 0.43) increased the calculated SFE of the 2.5 Al alloy by approximately 10%, but had little effect on the other two alloys. [b0021]
